en: *Prasādapratibhodbhava* (The *Śatapañcāśatka*) by Mātṛceṭa:
"He in whom no faults whatsoever exist at any time or in any way, and in whom all virtues abide through their complete manifestation. (1)

If one possesses discernment, it is right to go for refuge to him alone, to praise him, to worship him, and to abide by his very teaching. Furthermore, those faults along with their latent tendencies do not exist in that one Protector.
All [these] qualities are all-knowing and they are imperishable.
For no one, even if intent upon the actions of mind, speech, and body,
can find any discrepancy in the Blessed One that is inconsistent with the Dharma.
Thus, having attained this human state— a great festival of the True Dharma that is comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke in a vast ocean—
I have pursued impermanence while remaining in doubt regarding the gaps in my karma.
"How shall I make this Sarasvatī [speech] full of essence?"— thinking thus,
although one has understood the countless qualities of the Sage whose objects are immeasurable,
an exposition of only a single portion of them is undertaken out of respect for one's own purpose.
Homage be to you, the Self-Existent One, whose deeds are abundant and wondrous;
for whom there is no certainty regarding his qualities by way of either number or power.
There is no end to them such that one could say "they are this many," so what talk can there be of them being "like this"?
We are indeed talkative regarding virtues, saying "they are meritorious.
Yet, casting aside all consideration of whether something is endurable or unbearable,
you have yourself brought this world into a state of helplessness, where there is no one to cry out for aid.
You are a benefactor who has not been solicited; you are one who is affectionate without cause;

you are a friend to those with whom you have no prior acquaintance; and you are a kinsman to those who have never asked for your help. You have given even your own flesh—what need is there to mention other things?
O virtuous one, you have honored those who are dear to you even at the cost of your own life.
By means of your own bodies, you have purchased by the hundreds the bodies of living beings from those who sought to kill them; and by means of your own lives, you have purchased their lives.

Neither out of fear of miserable rebirths nor with the desire for a preferred destination did you make ethical discipline your second nature; rather, it was solely through the purity of your intention. This was achieved by constantly avoiding the crooked and constantly associating with the upright.
You have attained the state of being the sole path for the complete purification of karmas.
Though you were repeatedly oppressed, with a virtuous mind you revealed your splendor amidst the afflictions and showed compassion toward afflicted people.
The joy that arose within you as you were giving up your life for the sake of others— that would not arise in living beings even if their own lives were recovered after being lost.
This was so even when you were being repeatedly cut, indifferent to the pain.
O Lord, even toward sentient beings who were executioners, you felt compassion.
O Hero, you alone are the knower of the essence of that jewel of a mind, which is the seed of perfect enlightenment; other people are far removed from it.
"The state that is difficult to attain is not obtained without performing difficult deeds"—
thinking thus, you increased your vigor without regard for yourself. There was never a time when your commitment to excellence and preeminence faltered.
Therefore, in you, the sequence of degrees among particular qualities has been severed:
even attachment to very pleasant and fruitful meditative absorptions did not arise in your heart, which is perpetually bound by great compassion.
O one of noble conduct, that pleasure which is not shared by others— even if it be refined— only afflicts those like you and does not favor them;
yet from such a mixture, the essence is extracted and drunk entirely without stain.
What you have spoken well has been accepted by you, while what was ill-spoken has been avoided like poison.
O knower of the essence of jewels, you have purchased the well-spoken word even at the cost of your own life;
you have exerted yourself for awakening throughout those various successive births.
Thus, by striving in this manner for three incalculable eons, together with your resolve as your companion, you have attained the unsurpassed state—
without harboring envy toward those superior to you, and without disparaging those who are inferior.
Without engaging in rivalry with your equals, you have attained preeminence in the world.
Your attachment was directed toward the causes of virtues rather than their fruits;
therefore, through that correct practice, all virtues reached their perfection in you.
In this way, you have led your self to such a state of accumulation through your virtuous deeds that even the dust of your feet has attained the status of a sacred object of merit.
Having attenuated them, the faults were uprooted; having increased them, they were purified.

Through those virtues well-guided by you, you have attained supreme perfection. Thus, with a total assault, you have struck at the defects such that not even a trace of their latent impression remains within your own continuum.
Having thus gathered and accumulated these qualities within yourself,
they have been so established that even a mere semblance of them is not seen elsewhere.
They are subject to injury and obstruction, limited in time, and localized.
Every worldly object used for comparison possesses some degree of excellence;
but what comparison can there be for your qualities, which are free from duality, inaccessible, eternal, irreversible, and unsurpassed? (33–34)
The profundity of the salt ocean becomes as shallow as a cow’s footprint when it beholds the unfathomable and boundless profundity of your intellect;
the stability of earthly things becomes as light as the tip of a *śirīṣa* flower’s filament.
When your steadfastness regarding all phenomena has been made manifest,
O Sage, the sun does not find even the ground of a firefly within the range of your light of knowledge, which destroys the cataract of ignorance. (36–37)
The purities of autumnal moonlight, the sky, and water seem to attain a state of impurity in comparison to the purity of your speech, intellect,
and conduct. By this, everything that is virtuous in the world has been explained.
For the worldly ways of ascetics are far removed from the qualities of a Buddha.
O virtuous one, you have attained preeminence solely through the acquisition of that very jewel of the Dharma;
by that alone is there equality between you and it.
But when something that is merely a deceptive pretense born of self-interest, or some common secret matter,
is introduced and then discussed, that is the excessive fickleness of the speaker.
For as I reflect upon the nature of dharma, I perceive it to be exceedingly subtle.
And this entire world has been won over by you toward the victory over Māra.
For even when one is prepared to strike back out of great fury,
there is no burden too heavy for patience, especially when it is established in a worthy recipient.
That very great destruction of the afflictions which was accomplished on that very same night immediately following the victory over Māra— that indeed was most wonderful;
it was like the dispelling of darkness by the sun, garlanded with a thousand rays.
O Hero, he would be filled with amazement at your victory over the heretics:

the one full of passion defeated by the one free from passion; the wrathful by the one who has conquered anger; and the deluded by the one free from delusion—thus the three have been eternally conquered by the three.

You praise the true Dharma and censure the false Dharma; yet for you, there is neither partiality nor aversion toward what is good or bad. You harbor neither resentment nor attachment toward the Arhats nor toward the heretics.
What praise could there be for you whose mind is thus distinct?
You had no attachment even to virtues, nor any craving even for those possessed of virtue.
Oh, how pure is the nature of your perfectly serene being!
Through the constant clarity of your faculties, which never departs from you,
your mind is perpetually serene and appears as if directly perceived.
From childhood onwards, the purity of your intellect and memory has been well-known to all.
She was captivated by his well-spoken words and noble gestures, which revealed his inner state.
To whom would this form—not only tranquil and lovely, but also radiant and unassailable, both modest and majestic—not cast its spell? (51–52)
Whether it be one by whom [this form] has been seen hundreds of times, or one who beholds it for the first time, your eye delights in that form; for both of them, it is the same.
Indeed, because of its quality of being insatiable to behold and because of its gentle nature, your body—
At every sight, it bestows ever-new delight.

Your body is endowed with the qualities of its substratum, and your virtues with the qualities of their possessor; both are possessed of supreme excellence, mutually corresponding to one another. (54–55)
Where else could these qualities of a Tathāgata be so well-established,
except in this very form of yours, radiant with the primary and secondary marks?
Your form seems to say, "I am blessed," as it proclaims the virtues that depend upon it.
"Are we well-entrusted?"—as it were, his virtues replied thus.
"This entire world is bound without distinction by the afflictions;
you, however, have long been bound by compassion for the sake of liberating the world from its afflictions. (57–58)
Whom should I first revere: you, or Great Compassion, by which—even though you know such faults—you have remained for so long in saṃsāra?
For even though you are accustomed to the bliss of solitude, those [aeons] have passed for you while you were surrounded [by beings].
That which was done by you through compassion, having found its opportunity at the right time, is this:
for the sake of those to be trained, you are drawn from the peaceful forest to the edge of the village out of compassion, like a nāga from its lake by means of a spell.

Although you abide in supreme tranquility, being moved by the power of compassion, you have even set foot upon the arts of the actors and musicians. Whatever miraculous powers you possess, whatever lion’s roars you utter, and whatever manifestations of your own virtues there may be—
That compassion of yours is the touchstone for one who has vomited out the pursuit of desires;
O Protector, although your compassion—which is solely intent on the welfare of others—is indeed harsh toward its own support, it became truly non-cruel only in you. 63–64.
For indeed, having divided you into a hundred parts like an offering for some purpose, the wise ones have scattered you throughout the directions for the sake of accomplishing the aims of others;
yet it is clearly by your own will that she acts in accordance with them.
For even though she is reproaching you, she, being virtuous, does not commit an offense.
Her words are well-phrased, highly meaningful, truthful, and sweet; they possess both hidden and manifest meanings, and are characterized by both conciseness and elaboration.
Upon hearing such words as these from you, who could not be certain that you are omniscient, even if they were met with resistance?
For almost everything is sweet, and only by necessity is anything otherwise.
Indeed, every word of yours is well-spoken because it accomplishes your purpose.
Whether it be gentle, harsh, or endowed with both qualities,
all your speech attains a single flavor when subjected to scrutiny.
Oh, how supreme is the skill of these perfectly pure deeds,
by which such a vessel has been fashioned for these jewels of speech!
For from this [vessel], which is beautiful to behold, comes this [speech] which is enchanting to the ear.
From your mouth flows your speech like liquid nectar from the moon.
Your speech acts as a rain-cloud, pacifying the dust of passion;
it acts as Garuḍa in the matter of extracting the serpent of hatred.
It acts as the sun once more, dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
it acts as Indra’s weapon, shattering the mountains of pride.
Because its object is directly perceived, it is unerring; because it is free from afflictions, it is undisturbed.
For your speech is indeed "good in three ways" because it is well-composed and possesses the power of persuasion.
First, your words captivate the minds of the listeners;
then, when they are reflected upon, they remove both passion and darkness.
Your speech carries the yoke of yoga: it offers consolation to those in distress and terror to the heedless;
it inspires awe in those who are happy, generates joy for the wise, and increases the intellect of those of middling capacity. (77)
This speech of yours, which destroys the darkness of the dull-witted and is beneficial to all people,
draws Nirvana toward their vision,
draws them away from faults, extracts virtues, and rains down your words upon them.

Your intellect is unimpeded everywhere, your mindfulness is ever-present, and thus every one of your prophecies is unfailing in all circumstances. For you do not act toward those who are unworthy of instruction, nor at the wrong time, nor toward those who are unfit vessels.
Because you have exerted effort correctly, your word is unfailing.
Your teaching alone—the sole path, an easy means, self-conducive, and free from calamity—is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end; no other's teaching is so.
Thus, if fools, out of attachment to their own views,
revile that doctrine which is so entirely beautiful, there is no enemy equal to such a view—
[that view] for whose sake you have experienced the many calamities of the world.
Therefore, remembering that, you should remain even in a state of deformity within the teaching [of the Buddha].
How much more so, then, should the teaching of one who acts for your benefit and speaks for your benefit not be carried out by you, even if your head were on fire? (84–85)
Freedom from servitude, the bliss of awakening, the honoring of your virtues, and tranquility—
all this fourfold excellence is attained through your teaching.
It strikes terror into all non-Buddhist teachers and brings torment to Namuci.
O Hero, this command of yours is a source of consolation for the lords of men.
Your teaching has overcome the great domain of the three worlds— unimpeded and unrestrained— even the dominion of Death himself.
For one who knows the method of your teaching may remain even for an eon by his own will;
yet, being self-governing, he goes to that place where death has no jurisdiction.
[This applies] to the contemplation of the meaning of the scripture and to the cultivation of worship.

The distinction between the three times exists nowhere else but in your teaching. O bull among sages, what indeed could be more calamitous than this, that people do not honor this teaching of yours, which is so richly endowed with excellence? (90–91)
Hearing you brings satisfaction; seeing you brings clarity;
your speech gladdens; and your teaching liberates.
Your birth brings joy; your growth delights all beings.

Engagement bestows grace, while withdrawal strikes down [evil]. (93) Chanting your name removes sin; remembering you brings joy; seeking you sharpens the intellect; and full knowledge brings purification. (94)
Approaching you brings prosperity; serving you brings supreme wisdom;
honoring you brings fearlessness; and attending upon you brings auspiciousness. Purified by the perfection of virtuous conduct and serene through the perfection of meditation, [you are the refuge].
You are an unshakeable lake, a great reservoir consisting of merit, through the perfection of your wisdom.
Your form is a jewel to be seen; your well-spoken words are a jewel to be heard;
the Dharma is a jewel for investigation—for you are indeed a mine of jewels of virtue.
You are an island for those being swept away by the floods, a protection for those whose selves are wounded,
a refuge for those fearing worldly existence, and the ultimate resort for those seeking liberation.
You are a worthy recipient because of your pure conduct, and a fertile field because of the abundance of your fruit.
Because you act for their benefit, you are a true friend to all living beings.
Because you are dear to them, you are helpful; because you are pleasant, you are captivating.
Because of your gentleness, you are uniquely beloved and highly esteemed by all for your many virtues.

You are dear to the heart because you are irreproachable; you are delightful because of the excellence of your speech and form; you are blessed because all your aims are accomplished; and you are auspicious because you are the refuge of virtues.
You are the one who casts aside those who persist in error and the restrainer of those who seize what is right.
You are the restorer of those who have gone astray, the inspirer of those who move slowly;
you are the one who yokes the tamed to the burden and remains indifferent toward the wild.
Therefore, among those to be tamed by men, you are the unsurpassed and true charioteer. (102–103)
You have compassion for those in distress, a desire for their welfare when they are healthy,
kindness toward those in calamity, and a wish for the benefit of all; you maintain affection even for those who oppose you, and you exert yourself even for those who have fallen.

Compassion even toward those who are cruel—what indeed is this nobility of yours? If the status of being a guru is desired for parents because of their beneficence, then what kind of guru-status could there be now for you, who have been so exceedingly beneficial? 105–106.
Like selfs that are mutually opposed and indifferent to their own purposes, you have become a rampart for those standing on the edge of a precipice;
for the benefit of both worlds and for transcending the world. (107)
In worlds shrouded in darkness, the light of wisdom has been created by you.
The modes of enjoyment for gods and humans have been distinguished;
yet, through the commonality of the enjoyment of Dharma, they have attained non-differentiation in you.
O Blessed One, you have indeed established this universal hospitality toward all phenomena, which is free from the limitations of birth, age, color, place, or time.
You cause those who are not amazed to act as if they were amazed, and you inspire longing in those who are free from longing.
Those gods wait upon even the disciples with palms joined in reverence.
Oh, how radiant is the arising of a Buddha, the ornament of cyclic existence,
wherein even for the gods human birth has become an object of longing!
Weariness, the loss of the bliss of tranquility, association with the wicked, the pairs of opposites, and being crowded by distractions— bearing these faults,
you strive for the welfare of the world with an unattached mind. (113)

What indeed is this blessed *buddhadharmatā* of the Buddhas? (114) Even meager food was eaten at times, hunger was endured, uneven paths were traversed, and sleep was taken even upon thorny bushes. (115)

O Lord, even though you are the Sovereign, out of affection for those to be trained, you have undergone delays, concealments, service, and changes in dress and speech. O Lord, even your sovereignty is never found within yourself.
For you are indeed like one who must be spoken to by everyone; you are freely directed toward your own purpose.
By anyone at all, in whatever place and in whatever manner you may be urged, you do not overstep your own auspicious course of conduct.

People do not act with such benevolence even toward one intent on helping them, as you act with benevolence even toward one intent on harming you. Toward an enemy who brings about misfortune, you are a friend intent on bringing about their welfare.
Although you were constantly intent on seeking out faults, you were devoted to seeking out virtues;
for while your invitation was accompanied by poison and fire,
your journey there was compassionate and imbued with nectar.

Abusers were conquered by you through patience; those who sought to harm were met with well-wishing; those who spoke falsely were overcome by truth; and those who desired to kill were subdued by loving-kindness.
The many innate dispositions of men, which have been suppressed since beginningless time—
In an instant, you have transformed those whose misfortunes were manifested by you;
that the harsh became gentle, the miserly became generous, and the cruel attained kindness— that is your skill in means.
The pacification of the senses in Nanda, the humility of Mānastabdha,
and the forbearance of Aṅgulīmāla— who would not be struck with wonder?
(125) Many have abandoned beds of gold to lie upon beds of grass.
Those steadfast ones, satiated with the essence of Dharma, lay down in comfort.
Though questioned by anyone, you said nothing; even when approached, you did not engage in conversation.
Having quenched their thirst for the truth, you spoke to them in the next world, O knower of the proper time and disposition.

Having first generated excellence in the mind through discourses on generosity and other such means, the Dharma was then imparted, like dye upon a cloth free from stains. There is no means or power by which you have not exerted yourself.
In order to uplift the wretched world from the terrible abyss of saṃsāra,
you have appeared here and there with many diverse forms, words, and deeds, according to the varying dispositions of those to be trained. (129–130)
All these [deeds] are pure, uncontradicted, honored, and revered;
they are beneficial and exalted for both men and gods.
Indeed, it is not possible to speak or to perform much that is truly virtuous.
Both that which speaks otherwise and that which speaks not otherwise are seen in you.
By the purity of your self alone, the world would become purified;
for no such field exists within the three worlds as this.
How much more so for those who have utterly perished throughout the beginningless turmoil of existence!
You alone are thus exerted for the welfare of all sentient beings;
yet I know no such path by which I might repay your kindness. (134)

Even those who attain final nirvana are not free from their debt to you; for they remain established in your Dharma and act solely for their own benefit. As for the exertion undertaken for that purpose, what recompense can there be for it? (135–136)
For you remain awake, observing the continuities of those who sleep;
vigilant among the heedless beings, you are a kinsman of auspiciousness.
The destruction of the afflictions has been proclaimed, and the illusions of Māra have been dispelled.
The wretchedness of cyclic existence has been described, and the direction of fearlessness has been shown.
What else remains for one who desires the welfare of beings and is compassionate toward them, wherein you have not yet granted your approval? (138–139)
If these phenomena were mobile, they would certainly have been established by you everywhere, taking Devadatta as their basis.
For this very reason, O Lord of the World, here one thing is not the agent of another.
Thus you have spoken, as if making the world understand its true nature:
having long since impelled the True Dharma upon the earth out of compassion for the world, and having produced many excellent disciples capable of bestowing grace upon the three realms. (141–142)
Having directly disciplined the group of those to be trained, ending with Subhadra,
what debt toward sentient beings still remains for you today—
that you, grinding your bones into pieces as small as sesame seeds with the vajra of meditative concentration? (143)
Even at the end, you did not abandon your performance of what is exceedingly difficult to do.
You demonstrated to this world, which is so difficult to instruct, that both the Dharma-body and the Form-body are for the sake of others alone—even in your Nirvāṇa. (144–145)
For thus, having transmitted the Dharma-body in its entirety to those worthy recipients, and having broken your form-body into pieces as small as sesame seeds, you have entered final nirvana.
Oh, what a way of abiding! Oh, what conduct! Oh, what a form! Oh, what virtues!
Indeed, there is nothing at all that is not marvelous among the qualities of a Buddha.
Yet, even toward you—who are beneficial, pleasing to behold, and whose speech and bodily actions are peaceful—people show hostility; behold the ferocity of delusion! (147–148)
To those beings who pay homage to you— the ocean of merit, the treasury of jewels, the mass of Dharma, and the mine of virtues— to them also I offer my well-performed salutation.
(149) O Protector, your qualities are inexhaustible, whereas my power is limited.
Therefore, one remains because of the fear of [logical] consequence, not out of satiety.
You alone ought to know yourself by yourself—immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and invisible. (150–151)
Not even a fraction of a portion of your virtues has been proclaimed, yet supreme satisfaction remains in our hearts,
just as by not draining the waters of great lakes.
The thirsts of people indeed go to pacification by means of the arising of the fruit of this auspicious karma of mine,
which was produced through the inspiration of the sages' favor.
May the mind of the worlds, driven by the wind of unwholesome thoughts, come under control. // 153
